# PHP7 Installed by Homebrew Doesn't Work with Apache on macOS

When you install PHP via Homebrew on macOS, particularly on El Capitan (10.11), you often encounter a disconnect between the CLI interpreter and the web server module. You might run `php -v` in your terminal and see version 7.x working perfectly, yet accessing `localhost/phpinfo.php` in a browser results in a failure to load. The most common symptom is that swapping back to PHP 5 resolves the issue immediately, indicating the problem lies strictly within the Apache configuration rather than the PHP build itself.

The root cause usually stems from how Homebrew handles dynamic loading modules versus the default static linking found in system packages or older setups. When you install PHP with `brew install php`, Homebrew places a shared object file (typically named `libphp7.so` or similar, depending on the specific version and build flags) in your Homebrew cellar under `Cellar/php/...`. However, Apache does not automatically know how to load this new module.

In the provided configuration example from the pastebin, the issue is typically found in the `<IfModule>` blocks within your `httpd.conf` or a dedicated `LoadModule` section. If the line loading the PHP 7 module is commented out, or if Apache is attempting to load an outdated path that no longer exists after the upgrade, the server will silently ignore the PHP handler. This explains why you can see PHP 5 working: the configuration for the older version likely still points to a valid file path that Apache can successfully load.

To fix this, you need to ensure the `libphp7.so` module is explicitly loaded. Locate your main Apache configuration file, often found at `/usr/local/etc/apache22/httpd.conf` or `/etc/apache2/httpd.conf` depending on your setup. Look for the section handling PHP processing. You will likely see a line resembling:

```apache
LoadModule php7_module libexec/apache2/libphp7.so
```

If this line is commented out with a `#`, remove the hash mark to uncomment it. Ensure that the path `libexec/apache2/libphp7.so` actually exists on your system. If you installed PHP via Homebrew, the module might be located at `/usr/local/Cellar/php/.../lib/httpd/modules/libphp7.so`. In these cases, you must update the `LoadModule` directive to reflect the correct absolute path provided by Homebrew.

Another critical detail is the `AddHandler` and `AddType` directives. These tell Apache which files should be processed by PHP. If your configuration only contains handlers for PHP 5 (e.g., `.php5`), you must ensure that `.php7`, `.phtml`, or generic `.php` extensions are mapped to the new PHP handler. A typical pattern looks like this:

```apache
AddHandler php7-script .php
AddType application/x-httpd-php .php
```

Once these lines are corrected, restart Apache using `apachectl graceful`. Verify the fix by accessing your test script again. If you still encounter issues, check the error logs located in `/usr/local/var/log/apache2/error.log` for messages regarding "shared library" loading failures or missing dependencies.

It is also worth noting that Homebrew often installs PHP as an NTS (Non-Threading Server) build by default. While modern macOS versions handle this well, older configurations sometimes require the threading server (TS) variant if mixed with other modules. However, for most standard setups on El Capitan, ensuring the `LoadModule` path is correct and the handler directives are updated resolves the conflict between CLI and web environments without needing to reinstall PHP entirely.
